name: Mabenaro
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Guillaume, Antoine. 2021. Takanan languages. In Patience Epps & Lev Michael (eds.), Amazonian Languages: An International Handbook. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. HAL preprint halshs-02527795 (version of 13 Sept 2019), p. 4.
sources.note: Nothing about Mabenaro stress. Mentions it only as 'the possible existence of an additional, dead, Takanan language, †Mabenaro, known from a list of 54 words collected by the explorer William Farabee, published in Farabee (1922)', classified with hesitation by Girard (1971: 41-42). The chapter's stress discussion (§ on accent) covers Ese Ejja, Araona, Tacana, Reyesano and Cavineña only.

sources.citation: Loukotka, Čestmír. 1968. Classification of South American Indian Languages. Los Angeles: UCLA Latin American Center. Tacana stock, Mabenaro entry p. 176 and comparative table.
sources.note: Nothing. Entry reads 'Mabenaro - spoken on the Manuripi River. [Farabee 1922, p. 164.]' and a comparative table (head i-yoa, eye i-thaha, hand i-miatsa, fire kwathi, house ithai..) copied from Farabee without accent marks.

sources.citation: Créqui-Montfort, Georges de & Paul Rivet. 1921-1923. La famille linguistique takaná. Journal de la Société des Américanistes 13: 91-102, 281-301; 14: 121-167; 15: 121-157.
sources.note: Persée search matches 'Mabenaro' in the 1922 instalment (comparative vocabulary); worth checking whether the authors re-used Farabee's list and added any comment on it. Low expectation of any stress statement.

sources.citation: Farabee, William Curtis. 1922. Indian Tribes of Eastern Peru. Papers of the Peabody Museum of American Archaeology and Ethnology, Harvard University, vol. X. Cambridge, Mass.: Peabody Museum. Mabenaro section pp. 163-164.
sources.note: Nothing. The Mabenaro section is one page of ethnographic notes on two captured children plus a 54-word vocabulary (p. 164) written in Farabee's phonetic key; the page scan shows no accent marks on any word and there is no remark on stress or accent anywhere for Mabenaro (the only 'accent' hits in the book concern dancing). The author says he 'could obtain very little information concerning them or their language' and that it 'would seem that their language is very closely related to that of the Tiatinagua' (p. 163).

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 languoid record mabe1235 and reference record 24916 (Farabee 1922).
sources.note: Glottolog's fullest description is only a wordlist (Farabee 1922, 7 pp.); status extinct; classification Unclassified Tacanan; no other descriptive reference listed.
Nothing; states the language 'is known only from a list of 54 words which are not very well transcribed' (citing Girard 1971) and reproduces Farabee's kinship terms.

sources.citation: Girard, Victor. 1971. Proto-Takanan Phonology. University of California Publications in Linguistics 70. Berkeley: University of California Press. §5.2.2 'Mabenaro', pp. 41-45.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in (archive.org lending); the linked copy is not accessible
sources.note: The only work that discusses Mabenaro's phonology/transcription at any length (a classification section p. 45 and remarks that Farabee's list is poorly transcribed). Would confirm that no accentual information can be recovered, and is the source Guillaume 2021 and Wikipedia cite. Cannot contain a first-hand stress statement since its only Mabenaro data are Farabee's 54 words.

sources.note: Unknown. Persée's site search returns this article for 'Mabenaro' (comparative vocabulary of Takana dialects), but the PDF is behind an altcha challenge (automated download and direct download both refused, not reachable by automated download) and the landing-page text shows only the first vocabulary entries. Any Mabenaro data there would be Farabee's list re-used; not a stress source.
